titleEn: I will sing of the LORD's kindnesses forever
progression: | Dm Dm | Bb F | Gm A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: The longest psalm in Book III of the Psalter and the one that ends it. Ethan the Ezrahite, named in the heading, is listed among the wise men in the book of Kings, and the family name is usually connected with Zerah of Judah. The poem does three things in sequence: it praises the LORD for kindness and faithfulness, it quotes at length an oath granting David a permanent throne, and then it reports that the throne has been thrown to the ground, using the vocabulary of the oath to say so. It does not resolve. For a learner it is a drill in two forms: the suffixed noun (Your faithfulness, My kindness, his throne, our horn), and the second person perfect verb, which carries the entire accusation from verse 39 on. The last verse is familiar from the weekday evening service.

stichs.en: A maskil of Ethan the Ezrahite.

verses.summary: The heading names a singer who is not David, and marks the poem as a maskil, a psalm that teaches something rather than only praising.

stichs.en: I will sing of the LORD's kindnesses forever;
to every generation I will make Your faithfulness known with my mouth.

verses.summary: The vow comes before any argument. Kindness and faithfulness are the two words the whole psalm turns on, and both are given the widest span the language has.

stichs.en: For I said: kindness is built forever;
the heavens are where You set Your faithfulness firm.

verses.summary: The reason for the vow. Kindness is spoken of as a structure under construction, and the sky is named as the place the faithfulness is anchored.

stichs.en: I cut a covenant with My chosen one,
I swore to David My servant:

verses.summary: God begins to quote Himself. The covenant is introduced here in a single line and then quoted at length from verse 20.

stichs.en: Forever I will establish your seed,
and build your throne for every generation. Selah.

verses.summary: The content of the oath: seed and throne. These are the two items the last third of the psalm will report as broken.

stichs.en: The heavens praise Your wonder, LORD,
Your faithfulness too, in the assembly of the holy ones.

verses.summary: From the covenant back to the sky. The heavens that hold the faithfulness in verse 3 now answer with praise of their own.

stichs.en: For who in the skies ranks with the LORD,
who among the divine beings resembles the LORD?

verses.summary: The first rhetorical question. Nobody in the upper assembly is a rival, which is the ground offered for trusting the oath.

stichs.en: A God held in awe in the great council of the holy ones,
feared by all who surround Him.

verses.summary: The council of holy ones is a court, and the God who presides is feared by His own courtiers rather than merely obeyed.

stichs.en: LORD, God of hosts, who is mighty like You, Yah?
Your faithfulness surrounds You.

verses.summary: The question is put again by name, and answered as a fact of position: the faithfulness stands around Him like a retinue.

stichs.en: You rule the swelling of the sea;
when its waves rise, You still them.

verses.summary: The proof moves from the assembly to the water. Mastery of the swell is the standard demonstration of who actually holds power.

stichs.en: You crushed Rahab like a carcass;
with Your strong arm You scattered Your enemies.

verses.summary: Rahab is a name for the chaos monster of the sea. The victory is reported as finished business, which is exactly why verse 39 stings.

stichs.en: Yours are the heavens, Yours also the earth;
the world and all that fills it, You founded them.

verses.summary: Ownership follows conquest. Heaven and earth are listed as property, and the verb is founding rather than merely holding.

stichs.en: North and south You created;
Tabor and Hermon sing for joy at Your name.

verses.summary: Compass points, then two named mountains. The world answers from its corners and from its high places at the same time.

stichs.en: Yours is an arm with might;
Your hand is strong, Your right hand lifted high.

verses.summary: The arm of verse 11 returns as a permanent attribute rather than a single past act. The right hand here will be handed to the enemy in verse 43.

stichs.en: Righteousness and justice are the base of Your throne;
kindness and truth go before Your face.

verses.summary: The divine throne is described before the human throne is promised, and what holds it up is a pair of legal words, not force.

stichs.en: Happy is the people who know the horn blast;
LORD, they walk in the light of Your face.

verses.summary: The people appear for the first time. What makes them happy is not property but knowing a sound, the blast of the festival horn.

stichs.en: In Your name they rejoice all day,
and through Your righteousness they are raised high.

verses.summary: The joy is derived, not owned. The name and the righteousness are His, and only the lift belongs to them.

stichs.en: For You are the splendour of their strength,
and by Your favour our horn is lifted.

verses.summary: The horn is the ordinary image for a people's standing. It rises here only by favour, which is what verse 25 will promise the king.

stichs.en: For our shield belongs to the LORD,
and our king to the Holy One of Israel.

glosses: and to the Holy One of
verses.summary: The praise section closes by naming whose the king is. Shield and king are held by the LORD before any man wears either.

stichs.en: Then You spoke in a vision to Your faithful ones and said:
I have set help upon a warrior,
I have raised up one chosen from the people.

verses.summary: The oracle opens. Everything from here to verse 38 is quoted speech, introduced as a vision given to the faithful rather than to the king.

stichs.en: I found David My servant;
with My holy oil I anointed him.

verses.summary: The choice is told as a finding. David is discovered rather than produced, and the oil is said to belong to the sanctuary.

stichs.en: My hand will stay firm with him;
My arm too will strengthen him.

verses.summary: Hand and arm, the two words used of God in verses 11 and 14, are now put at the king's disposal.

stichs.en: No enemy will exact from him,
no son of wrongdoing will afflict him.

verses.summary: The first protection is phrased in legal and financial terms. The threat is a creditor with a claim, not only an army.

stichs.en: I will crush his foes before him,
and strike down those who hate him.

verses.summary: The protection turns active. The enemies are not removed from the world, they are dealt with in his sight.

stichs.en: My faithfulness and My kindness are with him,
and in My name his horn will be lifted.

verses.summary: The two key words of the psalm are attached to the king by name. This is the sentence the complaint will later hold up as unpaid.

stichs.en: I will set his hand on the sea,
and his right hand on the rivers.

verses.summary: The reach of the kingdom is measured in water. The king's hand is placed where God's own rule was demonstrated in verse 10.

stichs.en: He will call to Me:
You are my Father, my God, the rock of my rescue.

verses.summary: The bond is named as sonship, and the king's own words are quoted inside the quotation, a speech within a speech.

stichs.en: I too will make him firstborn,
highest of the kings of the earth.

verses.summary: Firstborn here is a rank conferred, not an order of birth. It gives precedence among kings rather than among brothers.

stichs.en: Forever I will keep My kindness for him,
and My covenant stands firm for him.

verses.summary: The promise is restated in the vocabulary of the vow in verse 2, with the covenant itself declared reliable.

stichs.en: I will set his seed to last forever,
and his throne like the days of heaven.

verses.summary: Seed and throne again, matching verse 5. The unit of time offered is the sky, which is the longest thing the poem can point at.

stichs.en: If his sons abandon My teaching,
and do not walk in My laws;

verses.summary: The condition begins. The covenant is written to survive failure by the descendants, which is the clause the later complaint cannot use as an excuse.

stichs.en: If they profane My statutes,
and do not keep My commandments;

verses.summary: The second half of the condition, moving from teaching and law to statute and commandment. Four legal words in two verses.

stichs.en: then I will call their rebellion to account with a rod,
and their guilt with blows.

verses.summary: The consequence is discipline rather than cancellation. The rod belongs to a father here, not to an executioner.

stichs.en: But My kindness I will not break off from him,
and I will not be false to My faithfulness.

verses.summary: The limit on the punishment. Whatever the sons do, the two nouns of verse 2 are declared non-withdrawable.

stichs.en: I will not profane My covenant,
nor change what went out of My lips.

verses.summary: Restated as a matter of speech. What has already left the mouth cannot be revised, which is the strongest form the guarantee can take.

stichs.en: Once I have sworn by My holiness:
I will never lie to David.

verses.summary: The oath is sealed on holiness itself. From here the promise carries no condition at all, and the psalm has staked everything on that.

stichs.en: His seed will last forever,
and his throne like the sun before Me.

verses.summary: Sun and moon are brought in as guarantors. The throne is set where it stays permanently in view.

stichs.en: Like the moon it will stand firm forever,
a faithful witness in the sky. Selah.

verses.summary: The oracle ends on the sky as witness, and the selah closes the quotation. The next word breaks the poem in half.

stichs.en: But You have cast off and rejected,
You have raged against Your anointed.

verses.summary: The break. The same You who founded the world has cast off, and every verb from here to verse 46 undoes something promised earlier.

stichs.en: You have renounced the covenant with Your servant;
You have profaned his crown to the ground.

verses.summary: The covenant of verse 4 and the anointing of verse 21 are both undone in one line, using the verb God swore not to use in verse 35.

stichs.en: You have broken through all his walls;
You have made his strongholds a ruin.

verses.summary: City imagery arrives. Walls down and strongholds ruined mean a military defeat, not a private grief.

stichs.en: Everyone who passes on the road plunders him;
he has become a disgrace to his neighbours.

verses.summary: The king becomes a roadside object. The specific injury is disgrace in front of the neighbours, which is what verse 51 comes back to.

stichs.en: You have raised the right hand of his foes;
You have gladdened all his enemies.

verses.summary: The reversal is exact. The right hand lifted high in verse 14 is now lifted for the other side.

stichs.en: You even turn back the edge of his sword,
and have not made him stand in battle.

verses.summary: The weapon fails and the man does not hold his ground. The help set upon a warrior in verse 20 is withdrawn in its own terms.

stichs.en: You have ended his brightness,
and hurled his throne to the ground.

verses.summary: The throne of verses 5, 30 and 37 hits the floor. This is the sharpest single contradiction between the oracle and the complaint.

stichs.en: You have shortened the days of his youth,
You have wrapped him in shame. Selah.

verses.summary: The last accusation is about time. Youth cut short and shame put on like a garment, and the selah lets the charge stand unanswered.

stichs.en: How long, LORD, will You hide Yourself forever?
How long will Your fury burn like fire?

verses.summary: The accusation becomes a question. Both halves ask how a state that is called permanent can be treated as temporary.

stichs.en: Remember what my lifespan is;
for what emptiness You created all the sons of man.

verses.summary: The argument shifts to human frailty. If a life is this short, delay is not neutral, it is fatal to the one waiting.

stichs.en: What man lives and does not see death,
who rescues his life from the hand of Sheol? Selah.

verses.summary: Frailty is made universal. Nobody outlives the wait, so a promise deferred past a lifetime is a promise withdrawn.

stichs.en: Where are Your former kindnesses, my Lord,
which You swore to David in Your faithfulness?

verses.summary: The direct demand, and it asks for the two nouns of verse 2 by name. This is the whole strategy of the psalm in one sentence.

stichs.en: Remember, my Lord, the disgrace of Your servants,
how I carry in my chest the insult of many peoples,

verses.summary: The petition widens from the king to the community. The disgrace of verse 42 is now carried by the servants and by the speaker in person.

stichs.en: with which Your enemies have taunted, LORD,
with which they taunt the footsteps of Your anointed.

verses.summary: The taunt is aimed at the anointed and therefore at the one who anointed him. The poem stops here, on the insult, with no answer given.

stichs.en: Blessed is the LORD forever.
Amen and amen.

verses.summary: This line closes Book III of the Psalter rather than the poem. The complaint is left open and the book is sealed over the top of it.

pardes.body: Three movements and a seam. Verses 2 to 19 are praise, built on two nouns, kindness and faithfulness, and on the claim that nobody in the divine council is a rival. Verses 20 to 38 are a quoted oracle in which God swears an unconditional throne to David, explicitly allowing the sons to sin and be punished without the covenant lapsing. Verses 39 to 52 report that the throne is on the ground, and they do it in the oracle's own vocabulary: covenant, crown, seed, right hand, sword, all reversed one by one. The hinge is a single word, {{39.0}}, and after it the You who founded the world in verse 12 is the You who broke the walls in verse 41. Nothing is resolved: the last thing the poem says is that enemies are mocking the anointed. Verse 53 is the doxology that closes Book III of the Psalter, so it seals the book rather than answering the poem.

The two nouns to track are kindness and faithfulness. Each occurs seven times, opening in the vow at {{2.7}} and closing in the demand of verse 50, where the speaker asks back for exactly what he sang about, which is why the psalm reads as a legal claim rather than a lament. Several cruxes stay open. In verse 3 the word rendered forever also means world, and the line has long been read both as kindness is built forever and as the world is built by kindness. At {{36.3}} the particle is literally if: a Hebrew oath states the first half of a self curse and leaves the rest unsaid, so if I lie to David functions as I never will. {{11.3}} is Rahab, a name for the sea monster of the creation combat and elsewhere a byword for Egypt. {{44.2}} is spelled like the ordinary word for rock, the same word the king uses of God in verse 27, and most readers take it here as the flint edge of a sword. {{48.3}} is a rare word for a lifespan, and the first half of verse 48 is broken enough that translators disagree about who its subject is.

An old rabbinic identification reads Ethan the Ezrahite of the heading as Abraham, which turns the psalm into a complaint made by the first man to receive a promise of descendants, and lets the oracle be heard as older than David. The reading of verse 3 as the world is built by kindness has had a long life outside this psalm, as a claim that creation is held up by acts of kindness rather than by law. Firstborn at {{28.2}} was taken as a rank granted rather than a fact of birth, and became one of the anchors of messianic reading here, since the throne promised in the oracle outlived every king who actually sat on it. The placement of the doxology at {{53.0}} was itself read as commentary: the book will not end on the taunt of verse 52, so it answers a complaint it cannot refute with a blessing instead of an argument.

In the kabbalistic reading the pair that governs the psalm, kindness and faithfulness, is a pair of measures rather than two moods, and the covenant with David is the tie between an upper throne and a lower one, so that damage below is spoken about as damage above. The hiding asked about in verse 47 is the standard term for the concealment of the face, a condition in which the relation is not cancelled but withdrawn from sight, which is what lets the psalm accuse and go on addressing at the same time. The throne thrown to the ground in verse 45 is read in this register as exile described from the divine side rather than the human one. The doxology at the end is then not a change of subject but the one move still available: to bless the source while the channel is shut.
